stem: Three students Arjun, Bhavna, and Chetan independently attempt to solve a problem. Their respective probabilities of solving it are 1/3, 1/4, and 1/5. What is the probability that the problem is solved by exactly one of the three students?

per_option_rationale.rationale: 3/5 = 1 - (2/3)(3/4)(4/5) = 1 - 2/5 is the probability that at least one solves it, not exactly one.
1/2 arises from computing only two of the three exactly-one cases and forgetting the third, giving an inflated sum.
1/60 = (1/3)(1/4)(1/5) is the probability all three solve it simultaneously, not exactly one.

explanation_sections.punchline: Exactly-one decomposes into three mutually exclusive cases - each student succeeds while both others fail.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify model: three independent Bernoulli trials, exactly-one query. Decisive move: enumerate three mutually exclusive cases. For each case multiply: (prob success) * (prob failure for other two). Sum the three cases. Do not use complement here since complement gives at-least-one.
explanation_sections.lesson: Exactly-k with independent trials: list C(n,k) cases, multiply within, sum across. Never use complement for exactly-k (complement gives at-least-k).
explanation_sections.timing: 90 seconds. Trap: 3/5 is at-least-one (complement of none). Trap: 1/60 is all-three. Need all three mutually exclusive exactly-one cases.
